title: Notes of Ministry - 50 - January 1977

paragraphs.text: 2 Kings 6: 25; 7: 1, 2; 1 Thessalonians 4: 14–17; Matthew 25: 31; Luke 10: 29–These verses are familiar, no doubt, to all who are here. A still more familiar passage of Scripture I would quote from John 3: 16, which is perhaps the best-known text in the Bible—“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whosoever believes on him may not perish, but have life eternal”. That is God’s proposal in the gospel. Man perishing, as men are all around, not only in the toll that years take, but perishing morally as estranged from God. What a cost that God should have given His only-begotten Son! He is going to have many sons eternally, sons by adoption. One, only-begotten, He gave! As to what is involved in that, I suppose, each one present would have some understanding, that that blessed Saviour who once lived here on earth was delivered up, as Peter says, “by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God”. As to man’s side, Peter went on to say, “Ye by the hand of lawless men, have crucified and slain”, Acts 2: 23. But He was delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God. That is a wonderful thing to keep in mind, that no one could have harmed Him, not only because of His own inherent power, but because God spared not His own Son but delivered Him up for us all (Romans 8: 32).

Nothing could be more important for any man than that he should believe on God’s only-begotten Son. Believe on Him where He is! Not only believe what you may have been told, or have read, about Him, but believe on Him where He is as glorified, as having the highest place there is, as being there, as one said very early in this dispensation, “as leader and saviour”, Acts 5: 31. As it also says, “neither is there another name under heaven which is given among men by which we must be saved”, Acts 4: 12. Must be saved!—conveying that God desires that you should be saved. Indeed, He desires that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. What need there is today to be saved!

What a situation exists in this city, and in every city in the world, corresponding with what we have read in the second book of Kings as to the situation that existed in Samaria where it says that the famine was such that an ass’s head was worth eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung five silver pieces. It is like the situation as it is today all around us. Men and women are feeding their minds on what normally would be repulsive.

They are in such a strait as perishing that they feed their minds and their souls on modern publications, and what comes to them through other sources of so-called entertainment, which bring with them moral death. So men and women are perishing! What a situation! The story we read records how a man in the position of highest opportunity, favour and privilege died without tasting the blessing that God brought into that beleaguered city. It is a solemn thing to die without tasting the blessing that God has brought in and is offering men today in the gospel. Present and eternal blessing is offered to us. Thank God, we can say humbly that we are speaking about that which we, know and prove, not a theory, not mere religion, but something which we know and prove.

We have known what it is to be perishing. Thank God, we came to recognise that we were perishing, but that God has given His only-begotten Son that whosoever believes on Him (without exception) might not perish. The price of salvation was paid by Jesus, the Saviour, by God’s Son, and there is nothing more for anyone to pay. All God looks for is the readiness to believe His word in the glad tidings, to believe on the Son, the Saviour, and if you do, surely you will repent. Every true preacher of the gospel presents Christ as Saviour, the only Saviour, and God commands all men everywhere to repent.

It may be that each one present would take the ground of being a christian. Sometimes persons are somewhat ignorant of the position and they say, I am not a Jew, I am not a Mohammedan, therefore I must be a Christian. Paul says in the word that we have read, “If we believe that Jesus has died and has risen again ...”. Do you believe that Jesus died and has risen again? Do you know Jesus? Not, ‘Do you know about Jesus?’. Not, ‘Do you wear a chain with a crucifix on it?’. I would ask whether you know Jesus. We prayed about this preaching, as we always do before the preaching, that God’s word might come. God hears the prayers that go up with regard to the preaching of the glad tidings. Without any self-advertisement—God forbid—I am assured that God has something to say to us in this place this afternoon by His word. We have the written word of God, and there is nothing like it in the world. God grant that every person here would read it. Read something of it every day of the week. Read it alone; however little time you may think you have to spend on it, read something. But believe on Him where He is, glorified, the One who died, and has risen again.

This is the witness that God is sending to men today. God is testifying to men that Jesus died and rose again. It is quite a challenge, you know, as to whether persons who hear receive God’s witness through the preaching, or through the written word of God; whether they really believe. If God speaks, man is responsible to believe.

If you believe that Jesus died and rose again, why did He die? Do you believe that it was because He brought error into the world, as His adversaries affirmed? Do you believe that He taught men to rebel against their religious customs? Do you believe that He taught men to break their allegiance to Caesar? The Spirit of God would bring home to you that nothing of that was the case. He did not die for any such offence. He died, I can say with the assurance of God-given faith, because I was a sinner and because, without Him, I should have been at a distance from God for all eternity. Man’s present condition is mortal, but man is the offspring of God and he can never be annihilated. The dead will be raised, every one of them. There is the first resurrection and the word says, “Blessed and holy he who has part in the first resurrection—over these the second death has no power”, Revelation.20: 6. There is a second death. One says, “I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne”, that is for judgment (Revelation 20: 12). After referring to the blest who have part in the first resurrection, the word is, “the rest of the dead did not live till the thousand years had been completed”. Then they will be raised. The apostle John saw it in a vision. The unreconciled dead will be raised for judgment and there will be no revocation of that judgment. How solemn it is!

We have read of a man who mocked at the promise of what was wholesome being available in plenty. He says, “If Jehovah should make windows in the heavens, would this thing be?”. And the next day it was so. That is a type of the present day when there is abundance, an abundance of divine blessing. I can assure you that it is so as having enjoyed it. I have enjoyed it with persons who are here. For many years now I have enjoyed it. The man who mocked died that day without tasting it. What a solemn thing! One says also, “How shall we escape if we have been negligent of so great salvation, which, having had its commencement in being spoken of by the Lord, has, been confirmed to us by those who heard?”, Hebrews 2: 3. This man mocked. You or I could be negligent. What a solemn thing to be negligent of so great glad tidings! You could hear nothing so great as God’s glad tidings concerning His Son.

I say, Why did He die? Paul says, in writing to his fellow believers, “Christ died for our sins, according to the scriptures”, 1 Corinthians 15: 3. We referred to this last week and remarked that they are the Old Testament Scriptures. I wonder if anyone has taken time to look up the Old Testament Scriptures referring to Christ dying for our sins. Then it says, “and … was buried”. He paid the penalty, the wages of sin, divinely ordained, “the wages of sin is death”, Romans 6: 23. I mention again what we read earlier in Hebrews 9: 27—“forasmuch as it is the portion of men once to die”—no one can dispute that; no mocker can dispute that! “and after this judgment”. Thank God that is not the end, for the writer goes on to say, “thus the Christ also … shall appear to those that look for him the second time”. Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many and to those who look for Him He shall appear the second time without sin, having nothing to say to sins, but for salvation, that is, the salvation of their bodies. What a prospect to be looking for Jesus, for the coming of Jesus! It
transcends every other hope and prospect, waiting for Jesus.

In this passage we have read from the letter to the Thessalonians. Paul says, “If we believe that Jesus died and has risen again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus”. That is the way to die, you know! And who knows who amongst us who may have died a week hence? Quite a question that, is it not? Paul puts it elsewhere, to depart to be with Christ, which is very much better (Philippians 1: 23). But then, Jesus is coming; He is coming in His glory. God used the evangelist Matthew to record Jesus saying that, “The Son of man comes in his glory” and shall “sit down upon his throne of glory”. That is what believers are looking for—Jesus coming in His glory! Paul puts it another way, he speaks of those who love His appearing. Oh how wondrous is the grace of God that persons who once may have loved unrighteousness are so transformed that they believe on Jesus, and now love His appearing! God-given faith assures them of the coming, the power and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul says, “so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus”.

How will He bring them with Him? Well, first He will come, as Paul goes on to say, “The Lord himself, with an assembling shout, with archangel’s voice and with trump of God, shall descend from heaven; and the dead in Christ shall rise first; then we the living who remain …”. If it should be tonight, you see, we should be above—“the living who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air; and thus we shall be always with the Lord”. I am looking to meet the Lord in the air. It does not say He is coming to the earth to take me up, but He is coming into the air. We believers shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the air and thus we shall always be with the Lord. What a prospect! No one has such a prospect as a believer in Jesus.

Is it yours? God would have it so. He would offer it to you in the glad tidings today; God is offering you all this blessing. The mocker may die without tasting that which has cost the sufferings of Calvary’s cross, cost the Saviour so much—His death, and the shedding of His precious blood which alone could remove the stain of sin before God. How comforting that is!
‘Were the whole realm of nature mine,
That were an offering far too small’.

The precious blood of Jesus alone could remove before God the stain of your sins and mine, and He did not draw back. He went into death and into the grave, as Paul says, “He was buried”. I am so thankful to know that, because I understand that He went into the grave for me as well as to the cross. The judgment and the punishment due to my sins He bore in His body on the tree; He bore God’s punishment due to me for my sins, all of them, but He was buried so that I never need mourn again the kind of man that I am by nature. I have known what it is to mourn the kind of man that I am, but I have been comforted to know that He was 4

buried. He took that kind of man out of sight into the grave so that God would be free to give me a new start and a new standing, not in Adam now, but in Christ, His own beloved Son. Blessed be His name!

So we are looking for Him. God is going to bring the dead saints with Him; when He comes He will raise them and He will catch them up to meet Him in the air and then very soon afterwards God will bring them with Him and, thank God, I shall be there. Will you be there?

The pleasure of God is that you should be offered this salvation this afternoon. Oh beware of mocking, beware of neglecting! What an alternative! Blessed are those in the first resurrection—but how solemn, “The rest of the dead did not live till the thousand years had been completed” (Revelation 20: 5), and then they are raised for judgment. Judgment is not part of the gospel, but it is the alternative, left in your sins, neglecting, maybe despising, the work of the one and only Saviour, Jesus, left to bear alone the penalty of your sins; how solemn! May God preserve every one present here from that!

You may say, Well, Paul wrote that and he has been dead many centuries; maybe I will have to wait for the rest of my time here with nothing but the hope. Oh no! that is why I have read from this well-loved passage in Luke’s gospel about the good Samaritan, as we call him, who came where the robbed and half-dead man lays And though the man was wounded, robbed, and half dead, he immediately poured in the oil and wine and, because he could not walk, supplied the power; he set him on his own beast. Many a sinner has had the oil and wine, as listening to God’s glad tidings and believing on the Saviour. He has felt the warmth of the wine being poured into him and then maybe he said, ‘I am so badly damaged that I cannot walk; I have no strength’. But the Saviour says, ‘I have the power of transport for you’. John the baptist said of the Saviour, ‘I have learned that He it is who baptises with Holy Spirit; I baptise with water, but I have had pointed out to me One who baptises with the Holy Spirit’.

Have you received the Holy Spirit? It is part of God’s promised blessing in the glad tidings that you should have the power to walk, though you may have been morally half dead. The Samaritan set him on his own beast and took him to the inn

and took care of him, and he stayed the night with him. Remember that; he did not go away immediately, he stayed the night with him. And on the morrow as he was departing he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper and said, “Take care of him, and whatsoever thou shalt expend more, I will render to thee on my coming back”. Do you understand the meaning of this? How we thank God for what the inn means and the One in charge, the Holy Spirit, who is commissioned by the Saviour to take care of me whilst I wait for Him to come.

Do you understand anything of the relations in such a place as is portrayed by the inn? It is a place of refuge, a place of light and warmth and life in the midst of the darkness, and the One over it has the resources and supplies to keep all who are in that inn—to keep them as God would have them preserved while they wait for the Saviour to come.

How I long to see Him! Do you long to see Him? Are you waiting for Him? There is no better occupation for any man than to be waiting—waiting for the Lord, loving His appearing, when He will appear in His glory, first having taken us, having caught us up and met us in the air, and then taken us into His own home, into eternal conditions. He might come before this day is ended and if He comes and catches up His own we shall be changed—changed into the conditions suitable to eternal glory. Even the dead in Christ are not in that condition yet, but if the Saviour comes today and they rise and are caught up to meet Him in the air, they will meet Him in a changed condition. There will be no grave clothes on any of them, and no grave clothes on us either who are living. We shall all be changed. Blessed prospect! And in the meantime, as I say, we have the light and the warmth and the spiritual comfort of the inn, the care of the One whose resources are sufficient to

maintain every one of His own, the blessed Spirit of God, and the believer’s hope, the coming of the Lord. May faith be found with each one of us to lay hold of this blessing for God’s glory, and for our present as well as our eternal blessing, for His name’s sake!
I have read these scriptures with a view to continuing what we have been considering as to having the absolute standard before us in Jesus. The reference in John 8 is indeed profound.

In speaking as He does, Jesus brings together in such a wonderful way the glory of His Person, who He is, and the perfection of His humanity, speaking of Himself as the One taught of the Father—not exactly what the Father taught Him, although it would be that, but as the Father had taught Him. He could say in John 20: 21, ‘ As the Father sent me forth, I also send you’. So here He brings in the glory of who He is in His eternal Person, the I AM, and yet along with it, “I do nothing of myself”. Think of what it says in Hebrews 1: 3 as to who He is—“the effulgence of his glory and the expression of his substance”, the One by whom God made the worlds, “upholding all things by the word of his power”, and yet the same glorious Person, the One whom they will have to recognise as the I AM, saying, “I do nothing of myself”. How glorious, how perfect, the humanity of Jesus! We can understand how the apostle Paul could say, “The mystery of piety is great. God has been manifested in flesh”, 1 Timothy 3: 16. God has come into these circumstances, come into these conditions, apart from sin, in all the perfection and glory of Jesus. “Ye shall know that I am”—God Himself—yet He could say, with only a comma between, “I do nothing of myself”; then there is the standard—‘ As the Father has taught me’.

I believe this would underlie what He says later, “He that has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14: 9). So perfectly did Jesus do and say things, not only what the Father did and said, but as He did and said them; what was seen in Jesus was the Father Himself.

These are matters which I feel we can say little about. How unique are the words of Jesus, more even than the inspired word, for they are the words of One who is God Himself. The prophets spake as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, by divine inspiration, but this is God Himself speaking in the Person of Jesus. “… ye shall know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself”. What can we say about it? but let us contemplate, for our souls, our affections, are moved by this glorious Person in the place into which He has come in this wonderful arrangement of love in which we are taught, and know by experience, that God is in the light: and “if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another”, 1 John 1: 7. Beloved, these things are to be the subject of our communion together in the holy fellowship—the glories of Jesus, the wonderful blend, may I say, of His Person and His humanity brought together by Himself, one might almost say two extremes—“I AM”, and then the dependence of His manhood, “I do nothing of myself”.
Now in John 13 we again have Him moving here

and we have portrayed before us not only what He did but how He did it, always remembering who it was that did it. John writes his gospel as having had the experience of this chapter, in the light of the present position of Christ in glory, and also in the gain of the presence of the Holy Spirit here. So as he wrote the first verse of his gospel it could well be that he would pause in the contemplation of this experience in John 13, thinking of who was there. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”

—John would pause and say to himself, ‘And He washed my feet!’. That is who was there in the glory of His Person, in the perfection of His humanity, “knowing that the Father had given him all things into his hands” (John 13: 3)—into those hands which Jesus employed in service to His own. But then it adds, “He came out from God and was going to God”. Of whom else could this be said but of this Person who is Himself God? He came out alone, but He has suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God, and here He is serving that, as returning. He might not return alone but that there might be those of whom He could say that they might have part with Him. So He rises from supper, you might say He divests Himself of all that was official, and having taken a linen towel girds Himself, and pouring water into the wash-hand basin begins to wash the feet of His disciples and to wipe them with the linen towel with which He was girded. How complete is the service of Jesus!

What refreshment it would bring. He says, “He that is washed all over needs not to wash save his feet, but is wholly clean”—fitted thus to have part with Himself—by His serving them in love. And when He had washed their feet He says, “Do ye know what I have done to you? Ye call me the Teacher and the Lord”—but then as Servant He had laid aside the garment of the Teacher and the garment of the Lord for the moment, that He might serve them in love. So He says, “If I therefore, the Lord and the Teacher”—never ceasing to be what He was on account of what He became—“have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another’s feet”. Much has been said about it, nor will I say much in enlargement on 7
the scripture, because I think it should remain in our minds freshly in its own beauty and power and effectiveness as simply going over it together.
Then He says, “As I have done to you, ye should do also”—not what I have done to you, but

‘ as I have done to you’. This is the divine standard of service. This is the level on which we should serve one another, rather than the official side. John does not here give us the official side, but he gives us this aspect, service in lowly grace in the infinite perfection of Jesus as He was here in service to His own that they might have part with Him. What can we say about it? What can I say about it, as to myself? but then it is here; what we may refer to as being abstract, as the standard, but concrete in this glorious Person—‘ As I have done to you’.

It is there, beloved brethren, that we might lay hold of it, that we might let the words of Jesus, the example of Jesus, by the Spirit have its own way in our hearts, that we might thus serve to refresh one another, to liberate one another, that we might have part together. He could say,

“Part with me”; for us it would be that we might serve one another in such a way that we would liberate one another, so that we can enter together into that of which we have been speaking together, that we may have fellowship together, in the precious knowledge that the blood of Jesus Christ, God’s Son, cleanses from every sin. That was how far He went to serve us. That was
what it involved for Him. John knew what He had done, for he witnessed the precious blood of Jesus coming from His pierced side.

I read in Acts 20 because there we have, not now the Lord Jesus, but the beloved apostle, a man of like passions to ourselves, and yet apprehended by the Lord from the glory that he might serve Him, that he might be a delineation. So we see in Paul one who could draw attention to himself; he says, ‘Ye know how I was with you’. Oh, dear brethren, how he would give an impression of Jesus as he moved amongst the saints. That is what Paul did. So what he leaves with this company is not just an impression of himself; the last words they hear from Paul are, “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive”. Mr. Taylor drew attention to the importance of every word of Scripture and how important each one is. I would commend it to the young, that if ever you are arrested by a word of Scripture that is not strictly necessary to the giving of the sense, then get to God and seek the help of the Spirit to understand why it is there. So it is not simply ‘He said’, but ‘He Himself said’—that is, that there should be no doubt. Paul is not drawing attention to himself; as he says, “We do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus Lord, and ourselves your bondmen for Jesus’ sake”, 2 Corinthians 4: 5. So the lasting impression that they would have would be of Jesus Himself, and any of us who have any little part in service—and all of us have some part, dear brethren, serving one another in obscurity it may be—should always serve in a way that leaves an impression of that glorious Person in all His perfection.

“It is more blessed to give than to receive”. Oh, how that was seen in Jesus! He could not have given more, and He would not give less, for He came to serve. What an incentive for us! We see the line of self-surrender set out in the service of the Master, and we are to follow in His steps. So Paul says, “Ye know how I was with you all the time from the first day that I arrived in Asia, serving the Lord with all lowliness, and tears, and temptations … how I held back nothing of what is profitable”. What concern he had for the profit of the saints, not seeking a place for himself. How we need to be preserved, dear brethren, from following men. We would have been preserved from so much in the past if we had kept before us what was brought out in those readings in Barnet in 1929, ‘The Divine Standard of Service’ (J.T. N.S. Vol. 29 p.330) in which the glory of the Person of the Son of God came out so distinctly.

Here the apostle is keeping that standard before the saints—‘He Himself said’—that is what Paul was labouring to bring before the saints, ‘ How I was with you’, and ‘ How I held back nothing of what was profitable to you’.

Then he says, “Yourselves know that these hands have ministered to my wants and to those who were with me”. He could draw attention to his hands. We spoke about the hands of Jesus, but here it is the hands of the apostle, serving so that he might not be a burden to them but that they might get the full gain of his ministry, that they might be liberated, and have part with him in the inheritance, related to a Man in glory. Then he says, “I have shewed you all things”, (Acts 20: 35); not ‘I have told you all things’, although he had set out the truth and taught them. But he had laboured, he had been from house to house, he had wept amongst them. He says, “I have shewed you all things”—it was not only what he had taught them, but what he had shown them. The beloved apostle was a demonstration. Nothing impresses young people more than a working

model. You might say that Paul was amongst these elders at Ephesus as a working model. He showed them all things. The great end of his labours was to leave an indelible impression of the glorious Person of Jesus, so he says, “He himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive”.

But then it is to be extended, so I read in Hebrews, “Remember your leaders who have spoken to you the word of God”. Thank God for those who have led amongst us. Let not what has happened to some in any sense detract from the Lord’s sovereignty in having raised up men of gift, especially those whom we speak of as leaders in the revival—such as the distinctive ministries of Mr. Darby, Mr. Raven, and Mr. Taylor. I believe what we had in London last October was valuable in relation to the Lord’s provision for our time. It has been a time when the saints have been recovered to the truth, and the truth was unfolded in a systematic way, bringing us to the recognition of the blessed Spirit Himself, the One who has served so constantly and consistently, so gloriously, all through this dispensation. We may not be able to trace that golden thread, but there it has been. The teaching that we had that He is not in the world but in the assembly is vital. There has been that under the eye of Christ, under the control of the Holy Spirit, an area where that service has been proceeding all the time. It says that “Christ also loved the assembly, and has delivered himself up for it”
(Ephesians 5: 25), and His service has continued all the time without a break because of the presence of the Holy Spirit here.

One of the crowning touches of the unfolding of the truth under those ministries was to bring us to recognise the distinctive place of the Holy Spirit Himself objectively, and what was due to Him in His holy Person. At one time it was said that we

would not again look for distinctive leadership as we had known it in those men; the Holy Spirit having brought us to that point in the recognition of Himself, we would go forward dependently on Him until the Lord came. I believe, dear brethren, that if we trace that as a point of departure in relation to the sorrows that have been amongst us in recent years, we shall have made some progress in our souls. That is a point to which the Lord is bringing us back, and to which the Holy Spirit is working at the present time to recover us, and I believe it is a point to which the beloved brethren are answering in recognising increasingly the place that the Spirit has in the opening up of the truth to us in the completing of these final touches in regard to the assembly’s history here, the final adornment in view of the day of presentation.
But I have digressed. “Remember your leaders who have spoken to you the word of God …

considering the issue of their conversation”. What did it lead to? What did their manner of life lead to? That is what we have been speaking about in the reading, “He that says he abides in him ought, even as he walked, himself also so to walk”, 1 John 2: 6. There have been men who have followed in His steps. They have walked in the light of the revelation, and where will that direct us? It will direct us to God Himself. God has come out. In that wonderful chapter, John 13, it says that He came out from God and was going to God. True ministry comes from God and will bring us to God. “Considering the issue of their conversation …

Jesus Christ … the same yesterday, and today, and to the ages to come”. Such men did not draw attention to themselves. In his letters, when in conflict as to the truth, Mr. Raven said he felt that the attacks on him were ‘utterly out of

proportion to the weight of the person implicated’ (‘Letters’ of Mr. Raven, N.S. pp.14 and 35), but thank God for those who have recognised the weight of what he said, and for the way that the truth that was recovered to us through his ministry has been revived in these latter days so that we are being brought together into the enjoyment of eternal life. It was not a question of making anything of himself, but directing the saint to Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, and today, and to the ages to come.

Leaders may come and leaders may go—and, sadly, we may say leaders may fail—but Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, and today, and to the ages to come. True ministry will lead to Him where He is, and that involves for us the full revelation of God—a Man in glory, the Holy Spirit here, and over all the Father in the supremacy of love—God known in Father, Son and Holy Spirit. What a great end to be reached! This is the way that the word will direct us. This is the way, I believe, that those whom the Lord has used walked and served, and as they spoke it would be with that attractiveness that would lead us to desire to know more of where they lived in the secret of their souls’ communion. We would love to know and be drawn into it. It is possible. This is what the end of their conversation would be. May we be drawn into it! Jesus could say in a perfect, unique, and distinctive way, “Come and see”, John 1: 39. Let us remember that. Let nothing of what has been said suggest that Jesus is anything other than absolutely unique in the glory of His humanity and in the distinctiveness of His Person. He could speak of “part with me”. The apostles came into it—the apostles’ fellowship—and they would be concerned that the saints should be brought into what they knew of the secret of divine purpose and counsel, and thus be brought into the knowledge of God Himself, as Paul says, “Until we all arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, at the full-grown man, at the measure of the stature of the fulness of the Christ”, Ephesians.4: 13. Well, may we be directed by what we have been considering here today. May we not lose sight of the standard; may we have nothing less before us, and may the Lord help us, for His name’s sake.
God, Thy power calls forth our worship,
As Thy works we contemplate,
Faith can know Thy word sufficient
All these wonders to create.
All the heavenly bodies tell it,
Held in orbit hour by hour,
Both the great and minute creatures
Witness the Creator’s power.
Then that power displayed in Jesus
In His pathway here we see;
Satan’s power gives way before Him
And his captives are set free.
He who had death’s might defeated
In the conflict of that hour,
Jesus risen; there we witness
All the greatness of God’s power.
Now the glorious Man ascended,
All in heaven His word obey;
Now His kingdom is established
Which in time He will display.
Though on earth He is rejected,
Faith can see His power appear;
Hades’ gates are not prevailing
Over His assembly here.
God attaches firmly to Him
Those subdued by Jesus’ power,
Learning more His love and kindness,
His protection every hour.
Here we learn the Spirit’s working,
Nowhere power on earth so great;
Yet He works in feeble vessels,
Those who humbly on Him wait.
Power for witness, power for service,
Power for overcoming here,
Then in access to the Father,
He the power for drawing near.
Soon the Lord will come in splendour,
‘Sun of righteousness’, He’ll rise,
All His foes shall fall before Him,
None can stand before His eyes.
Then His saints who’ve suffered with Him
Will the reigning with Him share;
Power that kept them through the suffering
Sets them in the glory there.
(Composed 1976)

It was the Lord’s desire, expressed to the Father, that we should be with Him—“that where I am they also may be with me”, John 17: 24. He knew that nothing less would satisfy the hearts of His own, so He says earlier that He would come again to receive us to Himself,

“that where I am ye also may be”, John 14: 3. The place is one thing—the Father’s house; but the assembly would never be satisfied without Himself. We must be with Him where He is, which is the greatest blessing, and the consummation of all.

So the Lord’s promise to the overcomer at Laodicea is to sit with Him in His throne. The Lord has sat down with His Father in His throne, thus inaugurating this wonderful period of grace. What wondrous equality is seen there, but His sitting down is on the basis of Himself having overcome. As Man He has overcome the great power of death and the grave. He is presented thus as the great Overcomer, having reached His present position on that ground.

He would sup with us here and we with Him, but He would have such with Him on His throne before the whole universe in the coming day wondrous answer to His grace! The thief was with Him that very day in paradise (Luke 23: 43). The one who overcomes now will be with Him soon upon His throne, and not just upon the throne but, as He says, “with me”
there.
Kingston, Ont.

A DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENT It was in a Swedish forest that we saw an astonishing sight—a large conifer growing out of a huge rock. Its roots must have penetrated through crevices in the rock and found nourishment deep down. It clearly illustrated how the work of God can flourish in very difficult circumstances—difficulties at school, at home, or at work, or, it may be, the difficulties of a local company facing smallness and isolation. The Lord Jesus grew up “as a root out of dry ground”, Isaiah 53: 2. He drew all His resources from another sphere, and those same resources are available to those who face difficult conditions as they seek to work out the truth. As we looked at that tree a brother from a very small meeting remarked that divine thoughts as to growth, spiritual prosperity, and formation are just the same for those in very limited and difficult circumstances as for those in what we might think to be more favourable positions.

For myself I would very much like to be in the rank and file of those who were seeking to meet the needs of His house. It might not be in any great way, perhaps, but still if it might be said as it was to the church of Philadelphia, “thou hast a little strength”; I would like to be little, and in the company of little people, but those who are seeking to minister “Meat in due season”, to His household. I think it might well be an ambition of every soul ...

The very fact that being here for Him is a pleasure to Him, and that as we blossom, and bud, and bring forth fruit. He is glorified, urges us to be more and more according to His mind. If I am only a daisy in a garden, and I know the owner of the garden prizes me very much, and likes to have me in his garden, and comes to see after me every day, and confers on me continually, like the shining of the sun, some special mark of his favour, do not you think that the little daisy will not be thinking of its littleness or uselessness, but of the unaccountable care, interest, and appreciation of the owner of the garden? He thinks of you, and He cannot love little. How the heart of the daisy, if it had one, would expand as it caught the approaching footsteps, in the daily visits of the owner.
The greatest earthly distinction that ever was given to any one is that of suffering for Christ.
